analysis: Lucy interpret's Mrs. Ferrars' coldness as a strategic victory, weaponizing 'civility' against Elinor.
The meeting of Elinor, Edward, and Lucy highlights Edward's paralysis vs. Elinor's polished performance.
Elinor's loitering on the landing-place represents the pinnacle of her self-sacrificing 'Sense'.
Marianne's praise of Edward's 'scrupulous conscience' creates a peak of dramatic irony.
The narrative contrasts Lucy's indifference, Elinor's ease of conscience, and Edward's middle-ground misery.
Edward's inability to speak reflects the stifling weight of Regency social and moral contracts.
The chapter deconstructs the 'civil' mask used by the social elite to hide prejudice and pain.
quotes: She had seen enough of her pride, her meanness, and her determined prejudice against herself...
Civil!—Did you see nothing but only civility?—I saw a vast deal more.
His heart had not the indifference of Lucy’s, nor could his conscience have quite the ease of Elinor’s.
Elinor... loitered away several minutes on the landing-place, with the most high-minded fortitude...
I really believe he has the most delicate conscience in the world; the most scrupulous in performing every engagement...
Poor Edward muttered something, but what it was, nobody knew, not even himself.
I cannot descend to be tricked out of assurances, that are not really wanted.
